title: 7 Christmas Stocking Mistakes That Waste Your MONEY (Fill It for $10)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, in nineteen fifty-one, my Christmas stocking held an orange, a handful of walnuts, a peppermint stick, a new pair of mittens, and one shiny silver dime. That's all. And it was the most exciting thing in the whole world. Danny and I were allowed to open our stockings before our parents woke up, and we sat on the stairs in the dark, whispering, for an hour.
scenes.query: old Christmas stocking orange candy cane
scenes.caption: ONE SHINY DIME

scenes.text: Today people spend a fortune filling stockings with plastic things that are broken by New Year's. So tonight I'm giving you seven stocking mistakes that waste money, and how to fill a stocking that people remember, for about ten dollars. And stay with me, because the last thing goes in the toe, and it's the one my grandchildren still talk about.
scenes.caption: ABOUT TEN DOLLARS

scenes.text: Our stockings were my father's old wool hunting socks, the long gray ones with a red stripe at the top, hung on nails on the edge of the piano, because we didn't have a fireplace. My mother darned the holes every December. Danny's sock had a patch on the heel shaped like Ohio. He was very proud of that.
scenes.caption: SHAPED LIKE OHIO

scenes.text: The legend of the stocking, honey, goes back to Saint Nicholas, a bishop in Turkey hundreds of years ago. The story says he tossed gold coins through a poor family's window for their three daughters, and they landed in the stockings drying by the fire. That's why there's an orange in the toe. It stands for the gold. In a minute I'll tell you the first mistake, and it's the size of the stocking.
scenes.caption: THE ORANGE IS THE GOLD

scenes.text: And make the stocking itself something special, honey. It doesn't have to be fancy. An old wool sock, a knitted one from Grandma, or a plain red felt stocking with each person's name stitched on the cuff in white yarn. Use the same one every year. When my son came home from college, the first thing he did was look for his stocking. It was the one from nineteen sixty-five, with a reindeer that had lost an eye.
scenes.caption: USE THE SAME ONE

scenes.text: Mistake number one. A giant stocking. The store sells stockings the size of a pillowcase, and then you spend forty dollars trying to fill it, and it still looks half empty. A smaller stocking, about eighteen inches long, filled to the top and overflowing, looks generous and exciting. A giant one half full looks sad. Small and stuffed beats big and empty every time.
scenes.caption: SMALL AND STUFFED

scenes.text: Mistake number two. All candy. A stocking full of chocolate and gummies is gone by breakfast, the children are bouncing off the walls, and nobody remembers it. Put a little candy in, a candy cane, a chocolate bar, a few chocolate coins. But fill the rest with things that last. Something to use, something to read, something to wear, and something to play.
scenes.caption: NOT ALL CANDY

scenes.text: That's my rule, honey. Use, read, wear, play. Something to use, like a new toothbrush, a fun pencil, a flashlight, or a tiny tool. Something to read, like a little paperback or a comic book. Something to wear, like warm socks, mittens or a hat. And something to play, like a deck of cards, a yo-yo, or a little puzzle. That fills a stocking for about ten dollars.
scenes.caption: USE, READ, WEAR, PLAY

scenes.text: Mistake number three. Wrapping every little thing in the stocking. It takes you hours on Christmas Eve, and the stocking is a mountain of torn paper by six in the morning. Wrap one or two special things, and leave the rest loose. Half the fun of a stocking is reaching in and pulling out surprises you can feel before you see them.
scenes.caption: REACH IN AND FEEL

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. And here's how to pack it, so it looks full and nothing breaks. Heavy, flat things go in the bottom, then the soft things, then the long things standing up, and the candy cane and something fun sticking out of the top. A stocking should look like it's about to burst.
scenes.caption: ABOUT TO BURST

scenes.text: Mistake number four. Only the children get stockings. Everybody in the family should have one, honey, even Grandpa. Grown-ups love stockings even more, because nobody's filled one for them in thirty years. Fill them with the little things they never buy for themselves. Good chocolate. Nice hand cream. A pair of warm socks. Lottery tickets. A little bottle of their favorite hot sauce.
scenes.caption: EVEN GRANDPA

scenes.text: My husband's stocking had the same three things every year for fifty years. A pocket knife, a tin of peppermints, and a pair of wool socks. He always acted surprised. Every year. When he passed, I found forty-two pocket knives in his dresser drawer. He'd kept every single one. I gave one to each grandchild at his funeral.
scenes.caption: FORTY-TWO POCKET KNIVES

scenes.text: So far, a smaller stocking, more than candy, use, read, wear and play, pack it right, and a stocking for everybody. Now mistake number five. All plastic things from the dollar store that break by lunch. Instead, look for little things with a story. An old silver dollar or a buffalo nickel. A marble. A pocket compass. A seed packet for spring. A little ornament with this year's date on it.
scenes.caption: THINGS WITH A STORY

scenes.text: And make some of it yourself, sweetheart. A little bag of homemade fudge or spiced nuts. A coupon booklet, handwritten. Good for one breakfast in bed. Good for one afternoon fishing with Grandpa. Good for staying up an extra hour. My grandson saved his coupon for a fishing trip for three years, and when he finally used it, he brought his own son.
scenes.caption: A COUPON BOOKLET

scenes.text: And fit the stocking to the person, sweetheart. For a little one, crayons, bath toys and a board book. For a teenager, earbuds, lip balm, a gift card and their favorite candy from when they were small. They'll roll their eyes and eat every piece. For a new mother, good tea, nice socks and a coupon for a nap while you watch the baby. That last one is worth more than gold.
scenes.caption: FIT IT TO THE PERSON

scenes.text: Mistake number six. Stockings hung where they can't hold the weight. People hang them on the mantel with little nails or flimsy hooks, and on Christmas morning, the whole stocking crashes down onto the hearth with everything in it. Use heavy stocking holders, weighted ones, or hang them on a sturdy chair or a staircase rail. Or lay them on the foot of the bed, the way the old families did.
scenes.caption: HANG THEM STRONG

scenes.text: And give everybody a little bag for the wrappers, honey. One paper bag per person, with their name on it. Christmas morning is hard enough on the living room without forty candy wrappers in the rug. My mother handed each of us a brown lunch bag on the stairs, before we touched our stockings. It's the only rule we never broke.
scenes.query: brown paper bags names Christmas morning
scenes.caption: A BAG FOR THE WRAPPERS

scenes.text: And now the last thing, the one my grandchildren still talk about. Mistake number seven is an empty toe. The toe of the stocking is where the very best surprise goes, the last thing you find. In the old days, it was the orange, for Saint Nicholas's gold. Put an orange in the toe, like my mother did. And next to it, one small special thing.
scenes.caption: THE TOE

scenes.text: In my grandchildren's stockings, honey, that small thing is a silver dollar. One every year, with that year's date on it. They don't spend them. They keep them in a little box, one for every Christmas of their lives. My oldest granddaughter has thirty-one now. She says when she's an old woman, she'll count them and remember every Christmas.
scenes.caption: ONE FOR EVERY CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: And for the grown-ups, sweetheart, a little handwritten note in the toe. Just a few lines, telling them one thing you're proud of them for this year. It costs nothing, and it's the thing they'll find last, after all the candy, when the room is quiet. My son found one from me in nineteen ninety-three, and he still keeps it in his wallet.
scenes.caption: A NOTE IN THE TOE

scenes.text: And one more old tradition, honey. In Grandma Pearl's day, a naughty child got a lump of coal in the stocking. My father put a piece of coal in Danny's stocking in nineteen fifty-three, after he set the porch mat on fire with a magnifying glass. Danny cried for ten minutes, until he found the real presents underneath. Today they sell candy coal, and it's a lot more fun.
scenes.caption: A LUMP OF COAL

scenes.text: And here's how I fill seven stockings without spending a fortune. I keep a shoebox in the closet all year. Whenever I see a good little thing on sale, a pair of socks, a deck of cards, a tiny flashlight, I buy it and drop it in the box. By December, the stockings are half done, and I never paid full price. My mother did the same thing with a pillowcase under her bed.
scenes.caption: A SHOEBOX ALL YEAR

scenes.text: So one more time. A smaller stocking, stuffed to bursting. Not just candy. Use, read, wear and play. Wrap only one or two things. A stocking for everybody, even Grandpa. Little things with a story, and some homemade ones. Hang them strong, and a bag for the wrappers. And an orange and a special surprise in the toe. That's the stocking people remember.
scenes.caption: THE STOCKING THEY REMEMBER

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. What was always in the toe of your Christmas stocking? An orange, a coin, something else? The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS IN THE TOE?
